opus-5.5.text:
So the core problem friend-shoring is trying to solve is that, in a pandemic, everyone needs the same things at the same time. Vaccines, therapeutics, diagnostics, and also the less glamorous inputs: lipids, bioreactor bags, glass vials, filters. What we saw during COVID was that when supply got tight, countries understandably looked after their own populations first. Export restrictions went up, contracts got renegotiated, and countries without domestic capacity ended up at the back of the queue.

So when I think about coordination among allies, the first thing I'd want is a shared, honest map of where capacity and chokepoints actually are. Not just finished-product manufacturing, but the whole supply chain. Very often you discover that a single country, or a handful of facilities, produce a critical input for everyone. You can't plan around a vulnerability you haven't mapped.

Second, I'd like to see deliberate specialization with guarantees built in. Not every country needs to make everything. That would be enormously expensive and duplicative. But if one partner is going to be the main source of a particular input, the others need confidence it will keep flowing in a crisis. So you want pre-negotiated agreements, ideally treaty-level or close to it, saying that in a declared emergency, partners won't impose export restrictions on each other for these specific categories. Without that, friend-shoring is just offshoring to a nicer address.

Third, there's the question of keeping capacity warm. Surge manufacturing capacity is very hard to keep alive in peacetime because there's no market for it. Allied countries could share that cost: jointly funding reserved capacity, running routine production of things like seasonal flu vaccines on platforms that can be repurposed quickly, and doing regular exercises so facilities and regulators actually know how to pivot.

That links to the fourth point, regulatory harmonization. If a product is approved and inspected in one partner country, there should be a fast path to accepting it in the others. Mutual recognition of manufacturing inspections and aligned emergency use pathways would save weeks or months, and in a fast-moving outbreak that translates directly into lives.

Finally, and this is important, friend-shoring can't become a club that leaves most of the world out. If a handful of wealthy allies lock up global capacity, you repeat the inequities of COVID and you also make everyone less safe, because a pathogen circulating widely elsewhere keeps evolving and comes back. So I'd want these arrangements paired with real investment in regional manufacturing in Africa, Latin America, and South and Southeast Asia, with technology transfer and fair allocation commitments. In a sense the best version of friend-shoring widens the circle of friends rather than narrowing it.

So: map the chokepoints, specialize with binding no-export-ban guarantees, share the cost of warm surge capacity, harmonize regulation, and build in equity from the start rather than as an afterthought.

r001.rationale: It recommends mapping supply-chain capacity and deliberate specialization, but does not clearly propose coordinating investments to fill gaps in what allies already produce.

r002.rationale: It proposes emergency agreements against export restrictions, but not reciprocal preferential trade terms for the medical countermeasures allies manufacture.

r003.rationale: It does not identify geographic proximity as making transportation easier during lockdowns.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the first thing I'd say is that friend-shoring, in the medical countermeasures context, is really about solving a trust problem rather than a pure manufacturing problem. We learned in 2020 and 2021 that when a crisis hits, export restrictions appear almost overnight, even between close allies. India restricted vaccine exports, the EU and the UK had their famous row over AstraZeneca doses, the US invoked the Defense Production Act in ways that effectively trapped inputs inside American borders. So the question isn't just "where are the factories," it's "what happens to the output of those factories when everyone is scared at the same time."

Given that, I'd want allied coordination to rest on a few pillars.

The first is pre-negotiated allocation agreements that are actually binding, or as close to binding as sovereign states will accept. If you're going to co-fund a fill-finish facility in, say, Canada or South Korea or Germany, the partners need to agree in peacetime how doses get divided in a pandemic, ideally on some transparent formula, population-weighted with adjustments for severity. If you leave that to be decided in the moment, you'll get the same scramble we saw last time, and the friend-shoring arrangement collapses exactly when it's supposed to deliver value.

The second is deliberately distributing different stages of the supply chain across different allies, rather than each country trying to build a complete end-to-end capability. The honest truth is that most countries cannot economically sustain a full domestic vaccine or monoclonal antibody supply chain in peacetime. The facilities sit idle, the skilled workforce drifts away, and politicians lose interest after a few years. But if the UK specialises in, say, mRNA drug substance, the Netherlands and Belgium in lipids and fill-finish, Japan in certain adjuvants, and so on, then each country has a sustainable commercial niche and a stake in the network functioning. You get redundancy at the network level without demanding redundancy at the national level.

Third, and this is the piece people underrate, is warm-base capacity. A facility that only exists for emergencies is a facility that won't work in an emergency. The regulatory validation lapses, the staff forget the process, the equipment isn't qualified. So allied governments should be jointly funding routine production, commercially viable things like seasonal flu or routine paediatric vaccines or even non-medical biologics, in these plants, so that there's a trained workforce and a current regulatory file that you can pivot. The Biomedical Advanced Research and Development Authority in the US has tried something like this with its Centres for Innovation in Advanced Development and Manufacturing, and the results have been honestly mixed, which tells you how hard it is. But the principle is right.

Fourth is regulatory harmonisation and mutual recognition. There's no point in having a friend-shored plant in Australia if a batch released there has to go through months of separate review before it can be used in the UK or Europe. The Access Consortium, the work the International Coalition of Medicines Regulatory Authorities does, these are the unglamorous mechanisms that determine whether friend-shoring actually functions at speed.

And then the last thing I'd flag is to be honest about the limits. Friend-shoring is still a form of partial exclusion. If the wealthy allied bloc builds a very resilient closed loop among itself, it may actually make the equity problem worse for the rest of the world, and that's both a moral problem and a practical one, because uncontrolled transmission anywhere generates variants that come back to you. So I'd want these arrangements designed from the outset with an explicit surplus-sharing obligation, so that the allied network becomes a platform for global supply rather than a fortress.

If you get those pieces right, the binding allocation rules, the distributed specialisation, the warm base, the regulatory plumbing, and the outward-facing commitment, then I think friend-shoring is a genuinely good idea. If you only get the factories built, you've mostly just bought yourself an expensive false sense of security.

r001.rationale: The response recommends co-funding facilities and distributing supply-chain stages among allies so each specializes in different capabilities instead of building a complete domestic chain.

r002.rationale: It proposes pre-negotiated allocation of pandemic doses, but does not propose reciprocal preferential trade terms for the medical countermeasures allies manufacture.

r003.rationale: It does not identify geographic proximity as an advantage for transporting countermeasures during lockdowns.

astra-6.text:
I’d like to see allied countries treat medical countermeasure manufacturing as a shared preparedness effort. Rather than every country trying to manufacture everything, you could have a network of countries with complementary capabilities and enough redundancy that the failure of one facility doesn’t undermine the whole system.

But the crucial question is what happens in a crisis. If one country manufactures the vaccines, another produces an essential ingredient, and another supplies the equipment, can they trust each other to keep those supplies flowing? Friend shoring only works if there are credible agreements about access, allocation, and export restrictions before an emergency begins.

So I would pair investment in manufacturing with joint procurement, coordination between regulators, and exercises that test whether the supply chain actually works. You also need to pay for capacity between emergencies. Otherwise, you’re asking companies to maintain something that may be essential for security but isn’t commercially viable year to year.

The aim should be a network in which countries gain resilience through cooperation, with clear commitments to deliver when that cooperation is put under pressure.

r001.rationale: The response describes complementary capabilities and shared investment, but does not clearly recommend directing investments to fill gaps in what allies already produce.

r002.rationale: It calls for agreements on access, allocation, and export restrictions, but does not propose reciprocal preferential trade terms among allies.

r003.rationale: The response does not mention geographic proximity or easier transport during biological-event lockdowns.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d like to see allied countries treat medical countermeasure manufacturing as a shared capability. That means coordinating ahead of a crisis: deciding which capabilities we need, where the bottlenecks are, and how we can distribute production so that we’re not all dependent on the same facility or the same supplier.

You don’t need every country to manufacture everything. You could have countries specializing in different parts of the supply chain, but with enough redundancy that a disruption in one place doesn’t bring the whole system down. And that has to include the less glamorous inputs—the raw materials, reagents, vials, and equipment—as well as the finished vaccine or therapeutic.

The crucial question is whether those arrangements will hold during an emergency. If governments impose export restrictions as soon as there’s a shortage, then having manufacturing in a friendly country doesn’t necessarily give you access. So you need agreements about allocation and supply, backed by joint procurement and investment, before the crisis happens. And you need to exercise those agreements, rather than simply assume they’ll work.

Ultimately, I’d want friend shoring to create a reliable manufacturing network that can expand quickly in a crisis, while also making countermeasures available beyond the countries that financed it.

r001.rationale: The response calls for joint investment and planning around capabilities and bottlenecks, but does not say investments should fill gaps in what allies already produce.

r002.rationale: It proposes allocation and supply agreements, but does not propose reciprocal preferential trade terms among allies.

r003.rationale: It does not identify geographic proximity or easier transportation during biological-event lockdowns as an advantage.
